opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest lesson is that whether a technique is a good idea in the abstract matters much less than whether it survives contact with how frontier models actually get built and shipped. A few criteria keep coming up.

The first is cost, and I mean all kinds of cost. Compute is the obvious one. If your method needs a forward pass with an extra probe, that's basically free. If it needs you to run a second model over every output, or retrain with a modified objective, that's a much harder sell. But engineering cost and complexity matter just as much. Frontier training and inference stacks are enormous, fragile, heavily optimized systems. Anything that requires touching many parts of that stack, or that someone has to maintain indefinitely, carries a real tax. Techniques that slot in cleanly at one point get adopted. Techniques that need everyone to change how they work tend to die quietly.

The second is the performance hit. If a safety technique makes the model noticeably worse, more annoying, or more prone to refusing reasonable requests, there's enormous pressure against it, and some of that pressure is legitimate. Users notice, and a less useful model is a worse product. So the bar is often something like: does this cost close to nothing on capabilities, or does it buy enough safety to justify the cost? Researchers often underestimate how strict that bar is.

The third is false positive rates, which I think is underappreciated, especially for monitoring. Something that catches 95% of bad behavior sounds great until you realize it also flags one in a thousand benign queries. At the scale these models are deployed, that's a flood of false alarms, and either a human has to review them or you're degrading the experience for a lot of innocent users. So in practice you care about very low false positive rates, and many techniques that look impressive in a paper fall apart there.

The fourth is evidence that it actually works on the real model, in the real setting. Results on a small open-source model or a toy task are a starting point, but the people making deployment decisions reasonably want to know whether this holds up on their model, at their scale, against their threat model. Methods that are easy to evaluate and easy to compare against simple baselines have a big advantage.

That connects to something I've become more convinced of: you should always compare against the boring baseline. Often a simple linear probe, a well-prompted classifier, or just reading the chain of thought does as well as, or better than, the fancy method. That's a bit humbling as an interpretability researcher, but a technique only matters if it beats what people would otherwise do. Being honest about that is key to being taken seriously by the teams that would deploy your work.

Finally, there's a human and organizational side. Techniques get used when someone inside the lab champions them, understands the constraints, and does the unglamorous work of making them production-ready. A good paper is rarely enough. You need someone who will turn it into a reliable tool, integrate it, and argue for it when tradeoffs come up.

So my practical advice to safety researchers who want impact is to think about deployment constraints early. Ask: Is this cheap? Does it hurt the model? What's the false positive rate? Does it beat simple baselines? Could a busy engineer adopt it without rewriting everything? If you design with those questions in mind from the start, your odds of mattering go way up.

r001.rationale: It says monitors need very low false-positive rates because even rare flags create many alerts on benign queries at deployment scale.

r002.rationale: It contrasts extra probes, running a second model on outputs, and retraining, but never says that adding fine-tuning data has much lower model-running cost than invoking another LLM on every query.

r003.rationale: It separates compute costs, such as running another model over outputs, from engineering complexity and ongoing maintenance costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because I spent a long time doing interpretability research in a fairly academic way, where the implicit goal was "produce a cool paper and get the field excited," and then I've spent a lot more time recently thinking about what it would actually take for any of this to show up in a model that ships. And the honest answer is that the criteria are much more mundane than I expected, and they're mostly not about how good the science is.

The first thing is that it has to be cheap. Cheap in compute, cheap in engineering time, cheap in the sense of not slowing down the training pipeline. If your technique requires some extra forward pass on every training step, or requires someone to retrain a bunch of infrastructure, you're competing with every other thing people could do with that compute and that engineer's time, and safety usually loses that fight unless it's basically free. A lot of the techniques that have actually been adopted are ones that look like a small plugin you bolt on at the end, rather than a redesign of how the model gets made.

The second thing is that it has to be something the people building the model can run without you. If the technique only works when a specialist stares at the outputs and interprets them, it's not going to get used at scale. It needs to be a number that goes into a dashboard, or a classifier that flags things, or something that fits into an existing eval loop. I think interpretability people, myself included, have historically underrated this. We produce these beautiful qualitative insights, and then someone on a product team says, great, what's the metric, and we don't have one.

The third thing, which is a bit uncomfortable, is that it helps enormously if the technique also makes the model better in some way that isn't about safety. If your thing reduces hallucinations, or improves instruction following, or helps debug a weird training failure, people will adopt it for that reason and the safety benefit comes along for free. If it's purely a cost that only pays off in a hypothetical bad scenario, you're relying on leadership caring enough to eat that cost, and that's a much shakier foundation.

And then the last one is just about timing and relationships. There are these windows where a team is deciding how to build the next thing, and if you have a technique that's ready at that moment and someone on that team knows you and trusts you, it can get in. If you show up six months later with a better version, the pipeline's already set and you're asking people to rip something out. So a lot of the practical work is less about having the best idea and more about having something good enough, at the right time, with the right people already convinced it's worth trying.

I don't want to be too cynical about this. I think the science does matter, and some things get adopted because they're just clearly correct. But if I were advising someone who wants their safety work to matter, I'd say spend way more time than feels natural on the boring stuff: making it cheap, making it automatable, making it useful for things other than safety, and actually talking to the people who'd have to run it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making techniques cheap and automatable, but does not mention false positives on normal user traffic.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the cost of adding fine-tuning data with invoking another language model on every query.

r003.rationale: It separately identifies engineering time and infrastructure changes as costs, and compute and added forward passes as ongoing pipeline costs relevant to adoption.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing that’s easy to underestimate is how much the practical details matter. It’s not enough to show that a technique makes a model safer in some setting. You need to ask: how much does it cost? Does it make the model less useful? Can you actually run it at the scale people care about? And does it give the team information they can act on?

For interpretability, for example, there’s a big difference between finding something interesting inside a model and helping someone make a decision. If you identify a feature that looks related to deception, what should they do with that? Does it reliably distinguish deceptive behaviour from a model discussing deception? Does it catch things that existing evaluations miss?

My takeaway is that you want to work backwards from a concrete use case. Find someone who has a safety decision to make, understand what evidence would change their mind, and build something that supplies that evidence. A modest technique that fits into an existing workflow and reliably catches an important problem can be much more valuable than an impressive demonstration that nobody knows how to use.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a technique costs much and reduces usefulness, but does not mention a safety monitor blocking harmful prompts or false positives on normal traffic.

r002.rationale: It discusses cost generally, without comparing fine-tuning data costs to invoking an additional language model for every query.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish implementation costs from ongoing model-running costs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing that’s easy to underestimate is how much the practical details matter. It’s not enough to have a technique that, in principle, makes a model safer. It needs to give the people building the model useful information or a useful intervention, at a cost they’re willing to pay.

So I’d ask: How much compute does this take? How much human time? Does it fit into the training and deployment process? Does it hurt the model’s capabilities? And, crucially, what decision would someone make differently because they used it?

With interpretability, for example, having an interesting explanation of what a model is doing isn’t automatically useful. If you can reliably identify a problem that existing evaluations miss, and that finding tells someone how to fix it—or gives them a concrete reason to delay deployment—that’s a much stronger case.

The standard also depends on what you’re asking for. A cheap diagnostic can be worth using even if it’s imperfect. Something that adds a large amount of training cost needs much stronger evidence. So I think safety researchers should spend more time understanding the actual decisions their work is supposed to inform, and testing whether it improves those decisions.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a safety monitor, false positives, or normal user traffic.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare adding fine-tuning data with invoking another language model on every query.

r003.rationale: It mentions compute, human time, and training cost, but does not distinguish implementation costs from ongoing model-running costs.
